course.title: Atomic – Cambridge Lower Secondary Science — Stage 8

unit.title: Light
unit.blurb: Luminous and non-luminous objects, how light travels, reflection and plane mirrors, refraction, dispersion by a prism, and coloured light.

O1.t: Describe light sources, beams and rays, the speed of light, and how materials transmit, reflect or absorb light.

O2.t: Describe reflection at a plane surface, use the law of reflection and describe images in a plane mirror.

O3.t: Describe refraction at air–glass and air–water boundaries in terms of the change in speed of light.

O4.t: Show that white light is made of many colours by dispersing it with a prism, and explain rainbows.

O5.t: Explain the colours of objects, and how coloured light can be added, subtracted, absorbed and reflected.

captions: Welcome to Atomic Education.
This lesson was written by the Atomic teaching team to
help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence.
Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 10: Light.
We see things because of the light they give out or reflect.
Why do soap bubbles shimmer with colours?
Modern lamps use reflection and refraction to waste less energy.
Let's explore how light behaves.
Light is a small part of a huge family of waves,
the electromagnetic spectrum, which also includes radio waves, microwaves and X-rays.
The colour of light depends on its frequency: red is lowest,
violet is highest. Mix all the colours together, and you get white light.
Objects that give out light are luminous.
The Sun is our main light source, powered by nuclear reactions.
Lamps and LEDs turn electricity into light, fireflies glow by bioluminescence, and lightning,
flames and lasers are luminous too.
Most objects are non-luminous: they don't make their own light.
We see them only when they reflect light from a source into our eyes.
That's why you can't read in the dark!
Light comes in beams, made of many narrow rays.
In a parallel beam, like a laser, the rays stay side by side.
In a diverging beam, like a torch, they spread out.
In a converging beam, like light through a magnifying glass,
they meet at a point called the focus,
which can be hot enough to start a fire!
Light travels in straight lines.
Look at a candle through three cards with holes in a row,
and you can see it.
Move one card out of line, and the candle disappears.
Shadows form for the same reason: a solid object blocks light's straight path.
Light is incredibly fast: almost 300 million metres per second in a vacuum.
Light from the Moon reaches us in 1.28 seconds,
and from the Sun in about 8 minutes.
That's why we see lightning before we hear thunder.
Distances to stars are measured in light years:
a light year is about 9.5 trillion kilometres.
Materials affect light differently.
Transparent materials, like clear glass, let almost all light through,
so we can see clearly.
Translucent materials, like frosted glass and sunglasses, let some light through,
but we can't see clearly.
Opaque materials, like wood and metal, let no light through.
When light hits a material, it can be absorbed, turning into heat; reflected,
bouncing off; or transmitted, passing through.
Dark colours absorb light well, which is why solar panels are dark.
And unlike sound, light can travel through the vacuum of space.

captions: When light bounces off a surface, it's reflected,
a bit like a ball bouncing off a wall.
The ray hitting the mirror is the incident ray,
and the ray bouncing off is the reflected ray.
The normal is an imaginary line at right angles to the mirror.
The law of reflection says the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection,
both measured from the normal.
The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal all lie in the same plane.
So if a ray hits a mirror at 35 degrees to the normal,
it's reflected at 35 degrees.
Smooth, shiny surfaces like mirrors give specular reflection:
all rays bounce the same way, making a sharp image.
Rough surfaces like paper scatter the rays in different directions:
this is diffuse reflection.
When you look in a flat, or plane, mirror,
light from you reflects off the mirror into your eyes.
Your brain traces the rays back in straight lines,
so the image seems to be behind the mirror,
even though no light comes from there.
So the image is virtual: it can't be caught on a screen.
It's upright, the same size as the object,
and the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front.
And it's laterally inverted: raise your right hand,
and your image raises its left!
A student shines a ray box at a plane mirror
and measures both angles from the normal with a protractor.
At 10 degrees the reflected ray is also at 10 degrees.
At 20 degrees she measures 21, and at 30 degrees she measures 29.
The points lie very close to a straight line through the origin,
where the two angles are equal.
Pause and decide: do her results support the law of reflection,
and why are some readings one degree out?

captions: When light passes from one material into another, it bends.
This is called refraction.
A ray entering a glass block bends once on the way in,
and again on the way out.
Refraction happens because light travels at different speeds in different materials.
It's fastest in air, slower in water and slowest in glass.
We say glass has a higher optical density.
When light slows down, it bends towards the normal.
When it speeds up, it bends away.
Think of a go-kart driving at an angle onto grass:
the wheel that hits the grass first slows down, and the kart turns.
If light hits the boundary straight on, along the normal,
it doesn't bend at all.
A coin lies at the bottom of an empty cup.
You move your head back until the rim just hides the coin.
Predict: what will you see if water is poured gently into the cup?
Pause and decide.
Watch. Your head stays still, and nothing changes while the cup is empty.
As the water is poured in, the coin comes back into view,
although you have not moved.
Explain what you saw.
Light from the coin travels up through the water.
At the surface it passes from water into air,
speeds up and bends away from the normal,
over the rim and into your eye.
Your brain traces the ray back in a straight line,
so the coin seems higher than it really is.
This is refraction. Pause and explain it in your own words.
Refraction can fool us.
Light from underwater speeds up as it leaves the water,
bending away from the normal.
So a pencil in water looks bent or broken,
and a fish looks closer to the surface than it really is,
which makes it hard to catch!
Refraction is also useful.
A camera lens is curved glass or plastic that bends light from
each point of a scene so the rays meet on the sensor,
forming a sharp image.
And stars twinkle because their light is refracted again and again by the changing air.

splitting white light into a spectrum of colours.

captions: A white card, a red apple and a green leaf are lit with white light.
Then the room is darkened and only a red lamp is switched on.
Predict: what colour will each object appear?
Pause and decide.
Watch. The white light is switched off and the red lamp is switched on.
The white card and the red apple both look red.
The green leaf looks completely dark.
Explain what you saw.
The only light arriving is red.
The white card reflects all colours, so it reflects the red.
The red apple reflects red too.
The green leaf reflects only green and absorbs red,
so no light comes from it to your eye.
Pause and explain it in your own words.
A non-luminous object's colour depends on the light it reflects.
A red apple reflects red light and absorbs all the other colours.
White objects reflect all colours, and black objects absorb them all.
Colour also depends on the light shining on it.
Put a blue object under red light: it absorbs the red,
and there's no blue light for it to reflect, so it looks black!
The three primary colours of light are red, green and blue.
Adding them together is additive colour mixing: red and green make yellow,
and all three make white.
Every screen is made of tiny pixels that mix red,
green and blue light.
Filters do the opposite: they absorb, or subtract, colours.
In subtractive colour mixing, the primary colours are cyan, magenta and yellow,
used in printing and photography.
Now it is your turn to shine!
Pause the video after each question and try to answer it first.
Question 1: Is the Moon luminous or non-luminous?
Pause the video now.
Answer: Non-luminous – it reflects sunlight.
Question 2: A ray hits a mirror at 50° to the normal.
What is the angle of reflection?
Pause the video now.
Answer: 50°.
Question 3: Why does a pencil look bent in water?
Pause the video now.
Answer: Light refracts as it passes from water to air.
Question 4: What colour do red and green light make when mixed?
Pause the video now.
Answer: Yellow.
